_link.title: I can compare ASD and ADHD in terms of similarities and differences

toLevel2.stem: Which feature do ASD and ADHD share?

options.text: Repetitive behaviours
options.explanation: Both ASD and ADHD can involve repetitive behaviours, though for different underlying reasons.

options.text: Difficulty with reading and spelling
options.explanation: Reading and spelling difficulties are features of dyslexia, not shared features of ASD and ADHD.

options.text: Identical brain structures
options.explanation: ASD and ADHD have different brain structures, even when behavioural symptoms overlap.

options.text: Preference for highly social environments
options.explanation: Impaired social communication is a feature of ASD, and neither condition is characterised by a preference for highly social environments.

toLevel2.stem: What primarily characterises ASD that distinguishes it from ADHD?

options.text: Impaired social communication and narrow interests
options.explanation: ASD is primarily characterised by social communication difficulties and narrow, focused interests.

options.text: Persistent inattention and hyperactivity
options.explanation: Persistent inattention and hyperactivity primarily characterise ADHD, not ASD.

options.text: Difficulty with reading and writing
options.explanation: Reading and writing difficulties primarily characterise dyslexia.

options.text: Creative problem-solving and impulsivity
options.explanation: Creative problem-solving and impulsivity are more associated with ADHD.

toLevel2.stem: What primarily characterises ADHD that distinguishes it from ASD?

options.text: Persistent inattention or hyperactivity
options.explanation: ADHD is primarily characterised by inattention or hyperactivity that disrupts functioning.

options.text: Impaired social communication and narrow interests
options.explanation: These are the primary features of ASD, not ADHD.

options.text: Distress over minor routine changes
options.explanation: Distress over routine changes is primarily associated with ASD.

options.text: Exceptional attention to detail
options.explanation: Exceptional attention to detail is a strength associated with ASD, not ADHD.

toLevel2.stem: Why might a person with ASD engage in repetitive behaviour?

options.text: As part of a narrow, highly specific interest
options.explanation: In ASD, repetitive behaviour is typically linked to focused interests or self-regulation.

options.text: Because of impulsivity or restlessness
options.explanation: Impulsivity and restlessness are the reasons for repetitive behaviour in ADHD, not ASD.

options.text: Because they have difficulty reading
options.explanation: Reading difficulties are a feature of dyslexia, not a cause of repetitive behaviour in ASD.

options.text: Because they are trying to disrupt others
options.explanation: Repetitive behaviour in ASD is self-directed, not aimed at disrupting others.

toLevel2.stem: What does 'comorbidity' mean in relation to ASD and ADHD?

options.text: That both conditions can occur in the same individual at the same time
options.explanation: Comorbidity means two or more conditions coexist in one person; ASD and ADHD are documented comorbid conditions.

options.text: That one condition always causes the other
options.explanation: Comorbidity means co-occurrence, not causation.

options.text: That the conditions are identical
options.explanation: Comorbidity means the conditions coexist, not that they are the same.

options.text: That having one condition prevents having the other
options.explanation: The opposite is true; comorbidity means both can be present simultaneously.

toLevel2.stem: ASD is primarily characterised by impaired social {{blank:1}} and narrow interests, whereas ADHD is primarily characterised by persistent inattention or {{blank:2}}.
Both ASD and ADHD can involve repetitive behaviours and difficulty adapting to certain {{blank:1}}, but their brain {{blank:2}} differ.
A person with ASD may repeat an action as part of a narrow {{blank:1}}, while a person with ADHD may repeat an action because of {{blank:2}} or restlessness.
ASD and ADHD have identical brain structures despite their overlapping behavioural symptoms.

options.text: True
options.explanation: This is incorrect. Brain structures differ between ASD and ADHD, even when behavioural symptoms overlap.

options.text: False
options.explanation: Correct. While ASD and ADHD share some surface-level behavioural similarities, the underlying brain structures are different.

toLevel2.stem: ASD and ADHD can both occur in the same individual at the same time.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Correct. Comorbidity between ASD and ADHD is documented, meaning both conditions can coexist in one person.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This is incorrect. ASD and ADHD are known to be comorbid conditions that can occur together.

toLevel3.stem: Both a student with ASD and a student with ADHD are observed fidgeting in class. How does understanding the underlying reasons help distinguish between the two conditions?

options.text: The student with ASD may fidget as a self-regulatory behaviour (stimming) linked to sensory needs, while the student with ADHD may fidget due to impulsivity and restlessness
options.explanation: The same surface behaviour has different underlying causes in each condition, which is key to accurate identification.

options.text: Both students fidget for the same reason, so no distinction can be made
options.explanation: The underlying reasons differ between ASD (sensory/self-regulation) and ADHD (impulsivity/restlessness).

options.text: Only the student with ADHD can fidget; ASD does not involve movement
options.explanation: Both conditions can involve repetitive movements, but for different reasons.

options.text: Fidgeting is not relevant to either ASD or ADHD
options.explanation: Fidgeting can be a feature of both conditions, making understanding the cause important.

toLevel3.stem: Why can surface-level similarities between ASD and ADHD lead to diagnostic confusion?

options.text: Because overlapping behaviours like repetitive actions and difficulty adapting may appear the same despite having different neurological causes
options.explanation: Similar behaviours can mask the different underlying conditions, leading to misdiagnosis if the cause is not investigated.

options.text: Because ASD and ADHD are actually the same condition
options.explanation: They are distinct conditions with different neurological bases, despite some behavioural overlap.

options.text: Because diagnostic tools cannot detect either condition
options.explanation: Diagnostic tools exist for both conditions; the challenge is distinguishing between overlapping symptoms.

options.text: Because only children can be diagnosed with these conditions
options.explanation: Both conditions can be diagnosed at any age; the confusion is about symptom overlap, not age.

toLevel3.stem: How do the social difficulties in ASD differ from any social challenges a person with ADHD might experience?

options.text: In ASD, social difficulties stem from impaired social communication itself; in ADHD, social challenges may result from impulsivity or inattention during conversations
options.explanation: The root cause differs: ASD involves fundamental social communication differences, while ADHD social issues are secondary to attention/impulse features.

options.text: People with ADHD have no social difficulties at all
options.explanation: People with ADHD can experience social difficulties, but these arise from different causes than in ASD.

options.text: Social difficulties are identical in both conditions
options.explanation: The causes of social difficulties differ between ASD and ADHD.

options.text: ASD involves no social difficulties; only ADHD does
options.explanation: Impaired social communication is a primary feature of ASD.

toLevel3.stem: What does it mean that brain structures differ between ASD and ADHD even when behavioural symptoms overlap?

options.text: That similar behaviours can have different neurological origins, meaning the same outward action may reflect different underlying brain processes
options.explanation: Different brain structures can produce similar-looking behaviours, which is why diagnosis must look beyond surface symptoms.

options.text: That brain scans cannot distinguish between the two conditions
options.explanation: Brain structure differences are documented; the point is that similar behaviour does not mean the same brain basis.

options.text: That brain structures are irrelevant to understanding these conditions
options.explanation: Brain structures are highly relevant and help explain why similar behaviours occur for different reasons.

options.text: That all neurological conditions have the same brain patterns
options.explanation: Different conditions have distinct brain patterns, which is why understanding neurology matters.

toLevel3.stem: How does the concept of narrow interests in ASD differ from the interest-dependent attention in ADHD?

options.text: ASD involves deep, sustained focus on specific topics as a core feature, while ADHD involves variable attention that is high for interesting tasks but low for uninteresting ones
options.explanation: In ASD, narrow interests are persistent and deep; in ADHD, attention fluctuates based on moment-to-moment interest.

options.text: Both conditions involve the same type of interest pattern
options.explanation: The patterns differ: ASD has stable narrow interests, while ADHD has fluctuating interest-dependent attention.

options.text: Only ADHD involves interest in specific topics
options.explanation: Both conditions involve interest, but ASD has deep narrow interests while ADHD has variable interest-dependent attention.

options.text: Neither condition involves interest in specific topics
options.explanation: Both conditions involve interest patterns, but they manifest differently.

toLevel3.stem: Why is understanding comorbidity important when assessing a person who shows features of both ASD and ADHD?

options.text: Because the person may have both conditions simultaneously, requiring support for both sets of challenges and recognition of both sets of strengths
options.explanation: Comorbidity means both conditions need to be addressed; treating only one may leave the person without complete support.

options.text: Because comorbidity means only one condition is real
options.explanation: Comorbidity means both conditions are present, not that only one is real.

options.text: Because comorbidity always requires medication
options.explanation: Comorbidity does not automatically require medication; support depends on individual needs.

options.text: Because comorbidity means the conditions will cancel each other out
options.explanation: Conditions do not cancel each other out; they coexist and both need to be understood.

toLevel3.stem: In ASD, social difficulties stem from impaired social {{blank:1}} itself, while in ADHD, social challenges may result from {{blank:2}} during conversations.
ASD involves deep, sustained focus on {{blank:1}} topics, while ADHD involves {{blank:2}} attention that depends on moment-to-moment interest.
Similar behaviours in ASD and ADHD can have different {{blank:1}} origins, which is why diagnosis must look beyond {{blank:2}} symptoms.
Repetitive behaviour in ASD and ADHD always has the same underlying cause.

options.text: True
options.explanation: This is incorrect. In ASD, repetitive behaviour is linked to narrow interests or self-regulation, while in ADHD it is linked to impulsivity or restlessness.

options.text: False
options.explanation: Correct. The same surface behaviour can have different underlying causes in ASD (focused interest) and ADHD (impulsivity/restlessness).

toLevel4.stem: A student repeatedly taps a pen during class. Their teacher is unsure whether this reflects ASD or ADHD. What information would help distinguish between the two?

options.text: Whether the tapping is linked to a specific sensory regulation need (ASD) or to general restlessness and impulsivity (ADHD)
options.explanation: Understanding the function behind the behaviour helps distinguish the conditions: ASD relates to sensory needs while ADHD relates to motor restlessness.

options.text: The volume of the tapping
options.explanation: Volume does not distinguish between ASD and ADHD; the function of the behaviour matters.

options.text: Whether the student is male or female
options.explanation: Gender does not determine which condition is present.

options.text: How often the tapping occurs per minute
options.explanation: Frequency alone does not distinguish between the conditions; the underlying reason matters more.

toLevel4.stem: A psychologist is assessing a child who shows poor eye contact and difficulty staying on topic. How should the psychologist approach the assessment given the overlap between ASD and ADHD?

options.text: Assess whether the poor eye contact is due to social communication difficulty (ASD) and whether staying off topic is due to inattention (ADHD), considering both conditions may be present
options.explanation: Each symptom should be traced to its likely cause, and comorbidity should be considered.

options.text: Automatically diagnose ASD because of the poor eye contact
options.explanation: Poor eye contact alone is not sufficient for diagnosis; other features must be assessed.

options.text: Automatically diagnose ADHD because of the difficulty staying on topic
options.explanation: Difficulty staying on topic alone does not confirm ADHD; the full picture must be considered.

options.text: Conclude that the child has neither condition because the symptoms are mixed
options.explanation: Mixed symptoms may indicate comorbidity; the child could have both conditions.

toLevel4.stem: A student with both ASD and ADHD (comorbid diagnosis) struggles in class. What approach should a teacher take to support this student?

options.text: Address both conditions by providing structure and predictability for ASD needs while allowing movement breaks for ADHD needs
options.explanation: Comorbid support requires addressing the distinct needs of both conditions simultaneously.

options.text: Only address the ASD because it is more serious
options.explanation: Both conditions need to be addressed; neither should be neglected.

options.text: Only address the ADHD because it is easier to manage
options.explanation: Both conditions need support; ignoring either one leaves the student without complete assistance.

options.text: Treat the student as neurotypical because the conditions cancel each other out
options.explanation: Comorbid conditions do not cancel each other; they coexist and both need support.

toLevel4.stem: Two students both have difficulty adapting to a new classroom arrangement. Student A becomes distressed and asks to return to the old arrangement. Student B becomes restless and starts moving around the room. Which pattern better aligns with ASD and which with ADHD?

options.text: Student A's distress over routine change aligns with ASD; Student B's restlessness aligns with ADHD
options.explanation: Distress over routine change is characteristic of ASD, while restlessness and difficulty settling is characteristic of ADHD.

options.text: Both patterns indicate ASD because they both involve difficulty adapting
options.explanation: While both involve adaptation difficulty, the specific responses point to different conditions.

options.text: Both patterns indicate ADHD because they both involve movement
options.explanation: Student A's response is emotional distress, not physical movement; this distinction matters for identification.

options.text: Neither pattern relates to ASD or ADHD
options.explanation: Both patterns are consistent with features of neurodivergent conditions.

toLevel4.stem: A parent reports that their child can talk for hours about trains (a specific interest) but cannot sit still during dinner. Apply your knowledge of ASD and ADHD to explain this pattern.

options.text: The intense focus on trains suggests a narrow interest characteristic of ASD, while the inability to sit still suggests hyperactivity characteristic of ADHD, potentially indicating comorbidity
options.explanation: The combination of narrow interests and hyperactivity points to possible comorbid ASD and ADHD.

options.text: This pattern can only be explained by ASD
options.explanation: The hyperactivity component is not explained by ASD alone.

options.text: This pattern can only be explained by ADHD
options.explanation: The narrow, specific interest in trains is more characteristic of ASD than ADHD.

options.text: This pattern is normal and does not relate to either condition
options.explanation: The combination of intense narrow interest and hyperactivity warrants assessment for both conditions.

toLevel4.stem: A case study describes a person who avoids social events and has difficulty making friends. How would you determine whether this is more consistent with ASD or ADHD?

options.text: Investigate whether the social avoidance stems from difficulty understanding social cues (ASD) or from impulsive social behaviour that has led to peer rejection (ADHD)
options.explanation: The underlying cause of social difficulty—communication impairment versus impulsivity—distinguishes the conditions.

options.text: Social avoidance always indicates ASD
options.explanation: Social difficulties can arise from different causes in different conditions.

options.text: Social avoidance always indicates ADHD
options.explanation: Social avoidance is more commonly associated with ASD, but can occur in ADHD for different reasons.

options.text: Social avoidance is unrelated to both conditions
options.explanation: Social difficulties can be features of both ASD and ADHD, though for different reasons.

toLevel4.stem: A clinician observes that a child shows both a smaller amygdala and delayed cerebral cortex maturation. What might this combination suggest about the child's diagnosis?

options.text: It could suggest comorbid ASD and ADHD, since a smaller amygdala is associated with both conditions while delayed cerebral cortex maturation is specific to ADHD
options.explanation: The combination of brain features from both conditions supports the possibility of comorbid diagnosis.

options.text: It rules out both ASD and ADHD
options.explanation: These brain differences are associated with ASD and ADHD respectively.

options.text: It confirms only ASD because the amygdala is involved
options.explanation: The amygdala difference is associated with both conditions; the delayed cortex maturation adds the ADHD component.

options.text: Brain scans cannot contribute to understanding these conditions
options.explanation: Brain structure differences are documented features of both conditions.

toLevel4.stem: Student A's distress over a routine change aligns with {{blank:1}}, while Student B's restlessness in response to the same change aligns with {{blank:2}}.
To distinguish ASD from ADHD in a case study, a psychologist should investigate the {{blank:1}} behind the behaviour, not just its {{blank:2}} appearance.
A child with comorbid ASD and ADHD needs support for both {{blank:1}} and predictability (ASD) as well as movement breaks and impulse {{blank:2}} (ADHD).

toLevel5.stem: Analyse why relying solely on behavioural observation without understanding neurological differences may lead to misdiagnosis between ASD and ADHD.

options.text: Because similar behaviours can stem from different neurological causes, and without understanding the brain basis, a clinician may attribute the behaviour to the wrong condition
options.explanation: Behavioural overlap between ASD and ADHD means that surface observation alone is insufficient for accurate diagnosis.

options.text: Because behavioural observation is never useful in diagnosis
options.explanation: Behavioural observation is useful but must be supplemented with understanding of neurological differences.

options.text: Because ASD and ADHD have no behavioural similarities
options.explanation: They do have behavioural similarities, which is precisely why additional understanding is needed.

options.text: Because neurological differences are always visible to the naked eye
options.explanation: Neurological differences require specific assessment methods; they are not visible through observation alone.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate the challenges of supporting a student with comorbid ASD and ADHD when the support needs of each condition may conflict.

options.text: Some strategies that benefit one condition may be counterproductive for the other, requiring careful individualised planning that balances both sets of needs
options.explanation: For example, reducing stimulation helps ASD but may worsen ADHD restlessness; support must be carefully tailored.

options.text: Comorbid support is impossible because the conditions are opposites
options.explanation: While some needs may conflict, individualised planning can address both conditions effectively.

options.text: One condition should always be prioritised over the other
options.explanation: Both conditions need attention; prioritising one and neglecting the other is not effective.

options.text: Comorbid conditions always respond to the same interventions
options.explanation: Different conditions may require different or even conflicting interventions.

toLevel5.stem: How does understanding the different neurological bases of repetitive behaviour in ASD versus ADHD improve the quality of psychological assessment?

options.text: It allows the assessor to identify the correct condition by tracing the behaviour to its neurological origin rather than relying on the behaviour's appearance
options.explanation: Understanding that the same behaviour has different neurological origins enables more accurate diagnosis and targeted support.

options.text: It eliminates the need for any assessment because the neurology is deterministic
options.explanation: Neurological understanding enhances assessment but does not replace it.

options.text: It proves that repetitive behaviour is always problematic
options.explanation: Repetitive behaviour can serve adaptive functions; the assessment determines its significance.

options.text: It has no impact on assessment quality
options.explanation: Neurological understanding directly improves the accuracy and quality of assessment.

toLevel5.stem: A school uses a single checklist to screen for both ASD and ADHD. Evaluate the effectiveness of this approach.

options.text: The approach is limited because a single checklist may capture overlapping behaviours without distinguishing the different underlying causes, leading to inaccurate identification
options.explanation: Overlapping symptoms mean that a checklist capturing surface behaviours cannot reliably distinguish between the conditions.

options.text: The approach is effective because both conditions have the same symptoms
options.explanation: While there is some overlap, the conditions have distinct primary features and neurological bases.

options.text: The approach is effective because checklists are always comprehensive
options.explanation: Checklists have limitations, especially when conditions share surface-level features.

options.text: The approach is unnecessary because schools should not screen for neurodivergent conditions
options.explanation: Early identification supports appropriate intervention; the concern is about the screening method's accuracy.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse how the different strengths of ASD (attention to detail) and ADHD (creative problem-solving) might complement each other in a team environment.

options.text: A team including individuals with ASD and ADHD could benefit from the detailed analysis provided by ASD strengths and the innovative ideas generated by ADHD strengths
options.explanation: The complementary strengths can create a more effective team when properly supported and understood.

options.text: ASD and ADHD strengths are identical and provide no complementary benefit
options.explanation: The strengths are different (detail versus creativity) and can complement each other.

options.text: People with ASD and ADHD cannot work together effectively
options.explanation: With appropriate understanding and support, their complementary strengths can enhance team performance.

options.text: Only neurotypical individuals contribute to effective teams
options.explanation: Neurodivergent individuals bring unique strengths that can enhance team effectiveness.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate whether current diagnostic practices adequately account for the high rate of comorbidity between ASD and ADHD.

options.text: Historically, diagnostic systems did not allow dual diagnosis, and while this has improved, the overlap in symptoms still makes comprehensive assessment challenging
options.explanation: Diagnostic practices have evolved but still face challenges due to symptom overlap and the complexity of comorbid presentations.

options.text: Current practices perfectly account for comorbidity with no issues
options.explanation: While practices have improved, challenges remain in accurately identifying and supporting comorbid conditions.

options.text: Comorbidity is too rare to warrant consideration in diagnostic practices
options.explanation: Comorbidity between ASD and ADHD is well-documented and needs to be accounted for in assessment.

options.text: Diagnostic practices should only ever identify one condition per person
options.explanation: Limiting diagnosis to one condition would miss comorbid presentations and result in incomplete support.

toLevel5.stem: A case study describes a young person who has intense knowledge about weather systems (discussing them in great detail) and who is also physically restless, frequently leaving their seat and interrupting others. Analyse which features align with ASD and which with ADHD.

options.text: The intense, detailed knowledge about weather systems aligns with ASD's narrow interests, while the physical restlessness and interrupting align with ADHD's hyperactivity and impulsivity
options.explanation: The case study clearly separates ASD features (narrow interest) from ADHD features (hyperactivity and impulsivity).

options.text: All features are explained by ASD alone
options.explanation: ASD explains the narrow interest but not the physical restlessness and impulsive interrupting.

options.text: All features are explained by ADHD alone
options.explanation: ADHD explains the restlessness and interrupting but not the deep, focused interest in a specific topic.

options.text: The features are unrelated to either condition
options.explanation: The features clearly align with documented characteristics of both ASD and ADHD.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate the importance of distinguishing between ASD and ADHD for developing effective support strategies.

options.text: Accurate distinction is essential because each condition requires different support approaches, and misidentification leads to strategies that may not address the person's actual needs
options.explanation: ASD support focuses on social communication and routine, while ADHD support focuses on attention and impulse management.

options.text: Distinction is unnecessary because both conditions require identical support
options.explanation: The conditions have different primary features and require different support strategies.

options.text: Distinction only matters for medication decisions, not support strategies
options.explanation: Distinction matters for all aspects of support, including environmental, educational, and social strategies.

options.text: Support strategies are the same for all neurodivergent conditions
options.explanation: Different conditions have different needs; one-size-fits-all approaches are less effective.

Accurate distinction between ASD and ADHD is essential because each condition requires different {{blank:1}} approaches, and misidentification leads to strategies that may not address actual {{blank:2}}.
